title: Fence Staining

h1: Brush-Applied Fence Staining That Actually Protects the Wood
intro: Spraying stain on fast is easy. Getting it to penetrate deep enough to survive a Southwestern Ontario winter is not. Restore My Deck brush-applies premium oil-based stain to every fence we work on, so it soaks in instead of sitting on the surface.
excerpt: Brush-applied, oil-based fence staining that penetrates deep and fades gracefully instead of peeling, in a range of transparent to solid finishes.

Premium oil-based stains: Ready Seal and Penofin Verde

included.title: Fence cleaning
included.body: Every fence is cleaned first to remove dirt, mildew and grey weathering, giving the new stain a surface it can actually bond to. See /fence-cleaning for that step in detail.

included.title: Repairs before staining
included.body: Loose pickets, popped nails or minor rot are addressed before staining so you are not sealing in a problem.

included.title: Drying time
included.body: We let the fence dry fully after cleaning before applying any stain, since trapped moisture is one of the main causes of poor adhesion.

included.title: Brush application
included.body: Stain is worked into the wood by brush rather than sprayed on, forcing it into the grain instead of leaving a surface film that will peel.

included.title: Two-coat process
included.body: Most fences get two coats for even colour and full protection, with time between coats for proper absorption.

included.title: Final inspection
included.body: Once dry, we walk the fence line checking coverage, colour consistency and any missed spots before calling the job finished.

body.text: Why We Brush-Apply Instead of Spraying

Spraying stain is faster, which is exactly why so many companies do it, but a sprayed coat mostly sits on top of the wood fibres instead of soaking into them. On a fence that faces a Kitchener-Waterloo winter, with freeze-thaw cycles that expand and contract the wood repeatedly, a surface coat is the first thing to crack and peel. Restore My Deck brushes stain into every fence we work on, working it into the grain by hand so it penetrates rather than sits. It takes longer, but it is the reason our stain jobs fade gracefully over years instead of flaking off in patches after one season.
The Stains We Use and Why

We work almost exclusively with premium, penetrating oil-based stains, primarily Ready Seal and Penofin Verde. Both are formulated to soak into wood fibres rather than form a plastic-like film, which is what lets them wear down evenly instead of peeling in sheets when they eventually need renewal. Water-based stains have improved over the years, but they still sit closer to the surface and tend to show wear faster on fences exposed to full sun, which describes most of the property-line fences we work on in this region.
Fence stain comes in a range of opacities, and the right one depends on how much of the wood grain you want visible and how much colour control you want.

items: Transparent: shows the most wood grain and natural character, with the least UV protection
Semi-transparent: our most requested option, balancing visible grain with solid colour and good UV protection
Semi-solid: more colour coverage while still showing some texture underneath
Solid: full opaque colour, closer to a paint-like finish while still penetrating the wood

body.text: Cedar and pressure-treated wood behave differently under stain, and we treat them accordingly. Cedar has a tighter, more consistent grain and generally accepts stain evenly with a shorter dry-out period, which is one reason it is a popular upgrade choice for new fence sections. Pressure-treated wood needs more time to off-gas moisture from the treatment process, particularly on newer installations, before stain will penetrate properly. We assess the wood on site and adjust the timeline and prep, including an 80-grit buff sand where needed, so the stain has the best chance of adhering fully rather than sitting on a surface that is not ready for it.

Most fence staining projects in Kitchener-Waterloo take about two days from start to finish, including cleaning, drying time, and two coats of stain. Larger properties or fences requiring more prep work can run closer to three days. We plan around the weather rather than rush a coat onto wood that has not had time to dry, since stain applied to a damp surface will not cure properly.

As a reference point, a standard 60-foot fence typically runs around $700 for staining, including cleaning, materials and labour. Every quote is confirmed on site since fence length, wood condition and access all affect the final price.
Weather Windows and Timing Your Project

Stain needs a dry surface and dry conditions to cure properly, which means Southwestern Ontario's shoulder seasons take some planning around. Spring brings frequent rain through April and into May, and fall can turn damp quickly once October arrives, so we watch the forecast closely and schedule staining jobs for stretches with at least a day or two of dry weather on either side of application. Summer generally offers the most reliable window, though very hot, direct sun can cause stain to dry too fast on the surface before it has fully penetrated, so we often time application for morning or early evening on the hottest days. None of this is guesswork on our end. It is part of how we plan every fence staining job from the first phone call.
How Often to Re-Stain a Fence

A properly brush-applied oil-based stain on a Kitchener-Waterloo fence typically holds up for five to six years before it needs a fresh coat, though south- and west-facing fences with more direct sun exposure may show fading sooner. Watching for the wood turning grey again, water no longer beading on the surface, or visible dryness are the clearest signs it is time to book another round.

faqs.q: Why do you brush-apply stain instead of spraying it on?
faqs.a: Brushing works stain into the wood grain instead of leaving it sitting on the surface, which is what lets it fade gracefully instead of peeling. It takes longer than spraying, but it holds up far better through our winters.

faqs.q: What stain finish is most popular for fences?
faqs.a: Semi-transparent is the finish most homeowners choose in our service area, since it shows the wood's natural grain while still providing solid colour and UV protection.

faqs.q: How often should a fence be re-stained?
faqs.a: Most properly stained fences in Kitchener-Waterloo need re-staining every five to six years, though fences with heavier sun exposure may need it a bit sooner.

faqs.q: Can you stain both new and older fences?
faqs.a: Yes. New pressure-treated fences usually need extra drying time before stain will penetrate, while older, weathered fences are cleaned and buff-sanded first to open the grain back up.

faqs.q: Can I choose a different colour or shade for my fence?
faqs.a: Yes, we offer a range of stain shades from transparent through solid in both Ready Seal and Penofin Verde, and can help you pick a tone that suits your property.

faqs.q: How long does the fence staining process take?
faqs.a: Most fences take about two days including cleaning, drying and two coats of stain, though larger or heavily weathered fences may take a bit longer.
